Therapy approaches | Motivational interviewing

Understand the hesitation before forcing a decision.

Motivational interviewing helps explore mixed feelings about change. Learn how collaboration, careful listening, and your own reasons differ from persuasion, pressure, or a therapist choosing for you.

See the worked exampleExplore clinician connections

The idea to keep in mind

Ambivalence is not automatically resistance.

Wanting change and fearing its costs can happen at the same time. The conversation makes room for both, while helping you hear your own priorities more clearly.

Understanding the approach

A guiding conversation, not a sales pitch for change.

Motivational interviewing is a collaborative communication approach that pays particular attention to a person's own reasons for change. It sits between simply directing someone and following without a focus. The practitioner listens for values, concerns, hopes, and uncertainty while respecting the person's autonomy.

Ambivalence means having competing motivations. A habit may cause problems and still provide relief, belonging, predictability, or something else important. Arguing only for change can miss what the person fears losing. A useful conversation explores those meanings instead of treating hesitation as a character flaw.

MI can be used within different services and therapies. It is not, by itself, a complete treatment plan for every concern. Information, assessment, specialist treatment, practical support, and a concrete plan may also be needed.

Sources mi psychotherapy

In plain language

Your reasons should be recognizable as yours.

A clinician can offer information with permission and raise concerns honestly. The process should not disguise the clinician's preferred choice as something you have independently decided.

A worked example

Less evening scrolling sounds good. Giving it up does not.

A fictional example of a low-stakes behavior change, not a guide to changing a substance-use pattern.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

Reasons to change

Avery wants more sleep and feels frustrated about losing an evening to a phone. They imagine being more present with family and less tired in the morning.

02

Reasons to keep things as they are

The phone is also a way to decompress after a demanding day. Avery worries that giving it up would leave them with chores, tension, and no time that feels their own.

03

A more useful focus

The conversation shifts from proving that scrolling is bad to understanding rest, choice, connection, and what Avery would be willing to try.

What might the clinician do instead of persuading?

A clinician could reflect both sides accurately and ask what matters most to Avery about a different evening. Avery may decide that the first priority is protecting actual downtime, not enforcing a stricter rule. Any plan would then need to address that priority instead of taking away the only available break.

This is a fictional illustration of autonomy and ambivalence. It does not imply that every habit can be changed safely without assessment or that a small experiment is the right response to a medically risky situation.

Sources mi psychotherapy

Go a little deeper

The skills support a relationship, not a persuasion technique.

Open questions, reflections, affirmations, and summaries are useful when they serve genuine understanding.

01Open questionsInvite detail that a yes-or-no answer may miss.Read more +

A question can explore what change would mean, what feels difficult, or what a person has already considered. Its value lies in the answer, not in steering the person toward an expected response.

A rapid series of questions can feel like an interview rather than collaboration. Listening between questions is part of the work.

02Reflective listeningCheck the meaning instead of immediately correcting it.Read more +

A reflection offers the clinician's understanding of what was said, including the tension between different wishes. The person can correct it. Good reflection is not simply repeating words or agreeing with everything.

It can make ambivalence easier to hear without arguing either side into silence.

03Your language about changeExplore desire, ability, reasons, need, and readiness.Read more +

A clinician may notice statements that point toward change and invite elaboration. They also attend to concerns about maintaining the current pattern. The aim is not to collect the right phrases as proof of compliance.

A person's readiness can differ from the importance of the goal or their confidence that change is possible.

04Planning when it fitsTurn a decision into a realistic next step, without rushing it.Read more +

When a person is ready, the conversation can move toward options and a plan. Permission-based information and shared consideration of barriers can help connect intention with action.

A premature plan may bypass the very uncertainty that needs attention. Not every useful session ends with a commitment.

Sources mi psychotherapy

Inside the work

Four overlapping tasks in an MI-informed conversation.

01

Engage

Develop enough understanding and trust to work together. The person should feel heard rather than managed.

02

Focus

Agree on what the conversation is about. A shared focus is different from a hidden agenda.

03

Evoke

Explore the person's own motivations, values, and concerns. Their reasons matter more than a persuasive lecture.

04

Plan

When appropriate, consider a next step that reflects readiness, resources, and barriers. The process can return to earlier tasks as needed.

Sources mi psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

Respecting autonomy and addressing risk can coexist.

Not manipulation

MI should not be used to obtain an answer the clinician has already decided is correct. Honest discussion of risks and professional recommendations is different from covert pressure.

Not sufficient for every treatment need

A collaborative conversation does not replace medical evaluation, crisis care, or a specialized treatment when those are indicated. In particular, changing some substance-use patterns can involve medical risks that require assessment.

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Does this mean the therapist never gives advice?

Not necessarily. Information and recommendations can be offered openly and with permission, with attention to what you understand and what matters to you. MI is not withholding useful knowledge; it is avoiding a tug-of-war over your choices.

What if I decide not to change?

Your autonomy remains important. The clinician may still discuss concerns or limitations of the service honestly. A session can clarify a decision without manufacturing commitment.

Is MI only used for addiction?

No. It is used in a range of behavior-change conversations. Its use in a setting does not make it a complete treatment for every issue in that setting. Ask how it fits the overall plan.

How is it different from solution-focused therapy?

MI particularly attends to motivation and ambivalence about change. Solution-focused therapy emphasizes a preferred future, exceptions, and useful differences. Both can be collaborative, but their focal questions are not identical.

Will every session end with homework?

No. Planning should fit readiness and purpose. Sometimes the meaningful work is clarifying why a change matters, what it might cost, or what support would make it feasible.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
